extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism, educators debating humanities vs. science, and general readers interested in culture
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating poetry and prose (what makes a 'classic' poem or a 'fit' prose) and for thinking about the role of literature and science in education and culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit prose — regularity, uniformity, precision, balance
rubrics_metrics.description: The needful qualities for a 'fit prose' are regularity, uniformity, precision, balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These qualities were necessary for the Restoration/ eighteenth-century prose project; an almost exclusive attention to them produces a prose suited to national needs but 'involves some repression and silencing of poetry.' Example contrast: Dryden and Pope are founders/priests of an age of prose and reason; their verse is admirable for that mission but lacks the fuller poetic criticism of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as criticism of life
rubrics_metrics.description: A true/ classic poem should provide an independent criticism of life — possessing matter and the inseparable manner of such criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay asks whether Dryden or Pope possess 'an adequate poetic criticism of life' and implies classic poetry must combine serious ideas with a poetic manner (gives examples of lines that indicate the right accent). Poetry that is merely skilled versification but lacks this criticism is not 'classic' poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: High seriousness / absolute sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: High seriousness, born of absolute sincerity, is essential to the poet's treatment of large ideas and gives poems moral and poetic power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay repeatedly emphasizes that application of ideas to life must be accompanied by 'the accent of high seriousness'; without it, passages that moralize or declaim lack the perfect poetic accent. Burns is criticized for often lacking this high seriousness except in rare moments of deep melancholy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of matter and truth of manner
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem should show 'truth of matter and truth of manner' — truthful subject-matter matched by an answering truthful style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The real Burns is described as having these truths in many pieces; where both align, the poetry is 'sound to the core.' This standard is used to distinguish genuinely successful poems from mere verbiage or bravado.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic largeness, freedom, insight, benignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities that mark great poetry include poetic largeness, freedom, insight, and benignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are listed as elements a classic poet's criticism of life should have; the essay contrasts poets (Gray, Chaucer, Burns) on these axes. A lack of these qualities marks verse as limited or provincial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness of style (poetry 'sound to the core')
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should have an answering truth of style so that the work is 'sound to the core.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soundness is shown by examples of Burns's lighter, arch pieces and by contrast with the more precarious 'beautiful haze' of Shelley. Soundness can make certain poets especially wholesome reading compared with others whose style is less grounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flawless manner and the 'perfect poetic whole'
rubrics_metrics.description: A flawless manner combined with other virtues produces a perfect poetic whole — an internally satisfying, unified poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: moments in Burns ('address to the mouse', 'Duncan Gray', 'Tam o' Shanter', 'The Jolly Beggars') where manner and substance combine to create masterpieces. The presence of a 'perfect poetic whole' is a marker of supreme poetic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classics as touchstone to correct personal/national bias
rubrics_metrics.description: When personal or national partiality distorts judgment, use the poetry of the great classics as a touchstone to correct estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay recommends comparing contemporary or popular estimates (e.g., of Burns) to the standards of great classics to reach a more objective, 'real' estimate. Collections of celebrated names/poems offer opportunities to apply this corrective method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture: know the best which has been thought and said
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim of culture is 'to know ourselves and the world' by knowing 'the best which has been thought and said in the world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the central educational aim; the phrase is discussed and expanded (Huxley quoted expanding it). 'Knowing the best' is not mere memorization of belles lettres but knowing the significant achievements of past and modern thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical/humanistic study must be 'scientific' — study originals
rubrics_metrics.description: A knowledge of classical antiquity is scientific 'when the remains of classical antiquity are correctly studied in the original languages.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolf's definition is cited: teaching is scientific when systematically followed to original sources. The essay stresses that genuine humanism involves rigorous, source-based study, not a superficial decorative 'belles lettres' approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include scientific results among what we must 'know' for culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing the best of modern nations includes what has been done by great observers and knowers of nature (Copernicus, Galileo, Newton, Darwin) — scientific results belong to culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responding to Huxley, the essay concedes that culture must include major scientific achievements; 'literature' in the broader sense includes books like Euclid's Elements and Newton's Principia, not only belles lettres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of natural science: habit of dealing with facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Study of natural science imparts the habit of dealing with facts via observation and experiment, which is an excellent intellectual discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay acknowledges that science's reality (we can be made to see experiments/results) contrasts with humanist knowledge, 'a knowledge of words.' This discipline is valuable and every one should have some scientific experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make natural science the exclusive staple for majority without considering human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Although scientific knowledge must be part of culture, it is questionable to make training in natural science the main part of education for the great majority without considering the constitution of human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues for caution: reformers propose making natural science primary, but this risks neglecting other human powers (conduct, beauty, social life). The writer prefers balancing claims of different human powers when designing education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance human powers in education: conduct, intellect, beauty, social life
rubrics_metrics.description: Human nature is built from powers of conduct, intellect/knowledge, beauty, and social life/manners; education must meet and adjust the claims of all these powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay uses this rough schema to argue that culture/education should not privilege one power at the expense of others. The humanities (letters) have a hold because they help relate pieces of knowledge to conduct and beauty, satisfying an instinct to connect knowledge with life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanities' integrative role — relating knowledge to conduct and beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Humans have a tendency to relate pieces of knowledge to conduct and to beauty; the humanities help satisfy this desire and thus hold a lasting place in culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay claims this integrative function explains why letters retain their importance: people seek to relate facts/intellect to the demands of conduct and to the sense of beauty; purely isolated factual knowledge can leave weariness and dissatisfaction if this relation is balked.
